story.title: Between Paper Margins and Digital Screens: How Omani Classrooms Are Rethinking the School Textbook
story.seo_title: Printed Textbooks and Digital Platforms in Omani Schools
story.meta_description: Omani educators and academics examine how combining printed school textbooks with digital learning platforms strengthens comprehension and self-learning.

detail.extracted_title: Between Paper Margins and Digital Screens: How Omani Classrooms Are Rethinking the School Textbook
detail.excerpt: As educational platforms and artificial intelligence reshape study habits, teachers and academics across Oman argue that deep comprehension depends on pairing the quiet focus of printed books with interactive digital tools.
detail.article_html:
In physics classrooms across Oman, the way a student prepares for an exam has changed noticeably over the past few years. Some students still open their printed textbooks, underline key definitions in pencil, and return to those marked pages the night before a test. Yet a growing number now reach for a smartphone or tablet first—searching for a short video explanation or an instant summary before even asking which page the lesson is on.

That shift sits at the center of an ongoing conversation among Omani educators and educational technology specialists. Rather than viewing printed books and digital platforms as rivals, teachers across the Sultanate point out that each medium trains a different habit of mind—and that students learn best when the two work together.

The Temptation of Instant Answers vs. Self-Learning

Physics teacher Muadh Al Mahrazi has watched students gravitate toward rapid, condensed reading. Out of impatience or fear of boredom, many skim headlines and pre-packaged summaries, or turn to artificial intelligence tools to generate immediate solutions without working through the underlying problem themselves.

While instant answers save time in the short term, Al Mahrazi warns that skipping the struggle of research and trial weakens long-term comprehension. To bring students back to the printed page, he advocates redesigning textbooks with built-in interactive challenges—such as crosswords, diagram-connecting exercises, and analytical puzzles—that turn the student into an active participant rather than a passive memorizer.

Bridging Divided Attention in the Classroom

For senior physics teacher Mohammed Al Khambashi, the most effective classroom is one where neither medium cancels out the other. The printed book remains the foundation for structured reading, analytical thinking, and organizing knowledge in a student's mind, while digital platforms contribute interactive simulations and visual clarity.

The main obstacle, Al Khambashi notes, is fragmented attention. Students often bounce between a screen and a book without settling into either, compounded by the belief among some learners that everything on the internet is accurate without checking primary sources. His solution is practical: update textbook editions over shorter cycles, ground physics and science problems in local Omani environments so students recognize their own surroundings in the lesson, and embed QR codes directly on printed pages to link paragraphs to verified simulations and exercises.

Spatial Memory, Handwriting, and Deep Focus

At Qamra Basic Education School, Assistant Principal Amal Al Hinai has observed a clear pattern in student performance. Over-reliance on ready-made summaries tends to produce temporary memorization, whereas students who regularly review their printed textbooks alongside digital resources show stronger analytical reasoning and deduction.

Dr. Maryam Al Shizawi, an academic specializing in educational technology and information science, explains the cognitive difference between the two environments. When a student opens a printed book, the mind enters a low-distraction space that builds "spatial memory"—anchoring an idea to its physical position at the top or bottom of a page. On digital screens, by contrast, the eye defaults to rapid scanning while expending mental energy to resist pop-up notifications and hyperlinks.

To help students benefit from digital abundance without losing depth, Dr. Al Shizawi recommends training learners to enter online platforms with specific, guided questions—and then encouraging them to summarize and rewrite what they read online in their own handwriting, locking digital information into lasting understanding.

detail.instagram_caption:
Across Omani classrooms, teachers are observing a quiet shift in how students study. While some learners still underline passages in their printed schoolbooks, many now jump straight to short video explainers, condensed summaries, or artificial intelligence tools for rapid answers before opening the lesson page.

Educators including physics teachers Muadh Al Mahrazi and Mohammed Al Khambashi, Qamra Basic Education School Assistant Principal Amal Al Hinai, and educational technology academic Dr. Maryam Al Shizawi argue that lasting comprehension depends on integrating printed books with digital platforms rather than replacing one with the other.

Printed pages offer a distraction-free environment that builds spatial memory and analytical patience, while QR-linked simulations, locally grounded Omani science examples, and handwritten summaries of digital research help students turn quick information into deep understanding.
